title: The thirst
hook: the second truth: suffering comes with craving (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was trained disciple: one who feels the first arrow of pain, not the second. Your line was skip the second arrow. Today, what keeps the bow drawn.

Drink salt water and you get thirstier. The very thing you reach for to fix the thirst feeds it. Other things work a bit like that. One more episode, and the next one starts on its own. One more look at the phone. One more thing in the cart. Each one is supposed to settle it, and each leaves the wanting a little wider. After it names suffering, the Buddha's first teaching names where suffering comes from, with a word for thirst.
screen: `SALT WATER MAKES YOU THIRSTIER.` → `ONE MORE, AND ONE MORE.` → `A WORD FOR THIRST.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali it's tanha, and the Pali-English Dictionary glosses it as thirst, and as craving: the same word does for a dry throat and a restless mind. Second, now here, now there. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the second noble truth says suffering arises with craving, bound up with delight and passion, seeking delight now here, now there. That's its restlessness. It doesn't settle on one thing and rest. It finishes one glass and looks for the next. Third, three thirsts. The same teaching names three kinds. A thirst for sense pleasures: tastes, sounds, touch, the good things. A thirst for being: to become something, to last, to be someone. And a thirst for not being: for something to stop, to go away, not to exist. That third one is easy to miss. Pushing away can be thirst, too. Wanting the feeling gone, the person gone, the day over, has the same dry, reaching quality as wanting more. Fourth, not every wish. Tanha doesn't mean wanting anything at all. The Buddha's own path asks for effort, and when a teaching on right effort describes the wish for wholesome states, it uses a different word, chanda. That wish isn't called thirst. The thirst is the grasping kind of wanting: the kind that can't stand still, and never quite says enough.
screen: `TANHA: THIRST.` · `NOW HERE, NOW THERE.` · `THREE THIRSTS.` · `NOT EVERY WISH.` · then, large: `THE THIRST.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and before long a pull will turn up: to check something, to move, to make this end. Don't feed it and don't fight it; look at it like thirst, noticing where it sits in the body, the chest, the hands, the jaw. Then stay, and watch what it does when it isn't fed.
Tanha: Pali for thirst, the craving the second noble truth names as where suffering comes from. For pleasure, for being, and for not being. Today's word.
Your line: now here, now there. Not every wish is thirst; the grasping kind is. Day seven hundred two.

howItsDone: Buddhists study the second noble truth as part of the four noble truths, and in meditation practice noticing craving as it arises, without acting on it or suppressing it.

fork.setup: you're sitting still, and a strong pull arrives to get up and check your phone. what does today's practice ask?

fork.reveal: feeding the thirst is the salt water. the practice is to look at it, where it sits in the body, and see what it does unfed.

original.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: thirst, craving. The Sanskrit form is tṛṣṇā.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says all desire is bad.
what it means: the second truth names a grasping thirst, now here, now there, as where suffering comes from.
what a scholar hears: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 lists kama-tanha, bhava-tanha and vibhava-tanha: craving for sense pleasure, for being and for non-being.

chat.says: So is wanting anything at all a kind of craving?
options: No, the thirst is the grasping kind; the wish for good states has another word.
Yes, this teaching calls even the wish for wholesome states thirst.
No, only wanting more counts; wanting a thing to stop isn't thirst.
chat.meaning: Tanha is the grasping, restless kind of wanting, including pushing away. The wish for wholesome states is called chanda, not thirst.

chanda.meaning: Pali for wish; used for wanting wholesome states

right effort.meaning: part of the Buddha's path: effort toward wholesome states

Pali.meaning: the old language of the Buddha's early teachings

notes: Editor: dictionary claim softened (PED lists 'drought, thirst; craving', so 'plain meaning first: thirst' and 'a body word before a mind word' were cut as unsupported etymology); chanda line now says only what SN 45.8 says; practice opener varied.

SN 56.11 paraphrased: the origin of suffering is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there: craving for sensual pleasures, for existence, for extermination (non-existence). 'Leads to renewed existence' is left out for length; confirm that omission is acceptable.
Pali-English Dictionary (PTS): taṇhā glossed 'drought, thirst; craving'. The script says the plain meaning is 'thirst' then 'craving'; confirm.
Right effort in SN 45.8 includes 'generates desire' (chandaṃ janeti) for wholesome states; the script uses this to say tanha is not every wish. Confirm the framing.
Salt-water image is the script's own, not from the texts.
Original: taṇhā in Devanagari (तण्हा), Sanskrit tṛṣṇā; confirm.
